questions.prompt: What makes a Sorted Set different from a plain Set?

options.text: Each member has a numeric score, and members are kept ordered by score
It is limited to integer values

questions.explanation: A Sorted Set keeps unique members, each with a floating-point score, ordered by that score — giving you a live ranking.

questions.prompt: Which command reads the three highest-scoring members with their scores?
questions.explanation: REV orders high-to-low so ranks 0–2 are the top three; WITHSCORES includes each score. Without REV you'd get the three LOWEST.

questions.prompt: Which statements about sorted sets are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: ZADD and ZSCORE are O(log N)
ZINCRBY atomically changes a member's score
The score can be used as a timestamp for range queries
Members can appear multiple times with different scores

questions.explanation: Core operations are O(log N), ZINCRBY is atomic, and scoring by timestamp enables time-range queries. Members are unique — a member has exactly one score.

questions.prompt: You need a priority queue where workers take the highest-priority job first. Which command fits?
questions.explanation: Use the score as priority; ZPOPMAX removes and returns the highest-scored member (BZPOPMAX blocks until one is available).

questions.prompt: To read members whose score falls in a range (e.g. a time window), use Z________ key min max. (complete the command name)
questions.explanation: ZRANGEBYSCORE returns members within a [min, max] score range (the modern equivalent is ZRANGE key min max BYSCORE).

questions.prompt: Match each command to what it returns.

pairs.right: A member's position counting from the top
The member's new score after adding to it

questions.explanation: ZSCORE gives the score, ZREVRANK the descending rank, ZINCRBY the updated score, and ZCARD the member count.
